name: Pale Grey
lede: Pale grey is a descriptive phrase for a grey close to white, and the swatch here is nearly paper white; the interest is in how books use the words.

sections.title: White that is really grey
sections.body: St Clair points out that products we call white are often technically very pale gray: Apple's "Moon Gray" headphones and keyboard plastic is her example [1]. The same glossary uses pale gray for other named shades, such as *French gray*, a very pale gray-green, and *glaucous*, a pale gray blue-green [2]. Neighbors on the page are [[light-grey]], [[dove-grey]] and [[pearl-grey]] [2].

sections.title: In the studio
sections.body: Pigment makers use the phrase for materials. Pumice is usually white, yellowish, pale grey or grey brown, and very low in density [3]. Coles notes that a lower-grade lapis lazuli ore gives a pale grey-blue pigment, which is why artists prized the purest stones [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is #FDFDFE, only a hair off pure white, so on a screen it reads as white [5]. A reader should treat the name as a range, from near-white to a soft mid grey, not as this single value [1][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the ColorHub archive, 342 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.4%, hold this near-white across at least 5% of the canvas, as photographed [5]. Every match is a highlight color [5]. Vincenzo Carducci stands out with 34 canvases, about 47 times the archive's average rate, and the rate is also high for Italy and Russia [5].

origin.source: St Clair, The Secret Lives of Colour
